text: A phantom read happens when your transaction runs the same query twice and gets back a different set of rows -- because another transaction inserted or deleted rows matching your criteria in between. The rows you already had don't change value -- entirely new rows appear, or ones you saw before vanish.
Session A opens a transaction and counts products priced between 500 and 1000. It gets back 14. That transaction stays open for a second query.
Session B inserts a brand-new product with a price in that same range, and it commits immediately. This row didn't exist at all when Session A's first query ran.

Session A runs the exact same query again, still inside its original transaction. This time it gets 15 -- a brand-new row appeared that wasn't there before. That extra row is the phantom: not a changed value on an existing row, but a changed set of rows entirely.

Here's the detail that trips people up. REPEATABLE READ holds locks on rows it has already read, which is exactly enough to stop a nonrepeatable read -- but Session B's new row didn't exist yet when Session A's first query ran, so there was nothing there for REPEATABLE READ to lock. Only SERIALIZABLE closes this gap, using a range lock that locks the entire range a predicate covers, not just the rows that currently exist -- so Session B's INSERT would actually be blocked.

That completes the three classic anomalies: dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads. Starting next lesson, we go through each of the six isolation levels in turn, starting with the loosest one of all -- READ UNCOMMITTED, where all three anomalies are possible at once. See you there.
